Mr. MEIGHEN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 23), to amend the Railway Act. He said:	The purpose of this
Bill is, to deal with the old question of the loss caused by animals getting on the railway right of way. The section which it is proposed to amend is subsection 4 of section 294 of the Railway Act. Under provisions of this section tire railway company is made prima facie liable in the case of losses of this kind. Such is the state of the law and of the amendment that was adopted last session, that a railway company are able to escape liability by proving that the animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act of the owner. The amendment which I propose alters that provision. At the present time the burden of proof of negligence is on the railway company, and they must prove that the owner of the animal was guilty of negligence or of a wilful act in allowing the animal out. The burden of
proof is not shifted by the amendment, but the nature of the proof is altered, compelling the railway company to prove that the animal got upon their right of way without negligence on _ their part and without violation of the provisions of the law. The amendment further alters section 254. Subsection 2 is specific in the matter of fences and gates, it is specific as to their size; and in the matter of cattle-guards, it is also specific as to what they must accomplish. It says nothing about their nature, their construction or dimensions. The present amendment compels the railway companies, before a fixed time, to submit the nature, dimensions and construction of their cattle-guards to the Board of Railway Commissioners for its approval. The effect will be that if a railway company complies with the specific dimensions prescribed by the Board they will be absolved; but they must so comply and if they fail to comply they will not be able to throw back the liability on some one who perhaps was negligent, but more remotely negligent than the company; that is to say, they will apply the general law to themselves in cases of damage, and the party who is immediately responsible for negligence will be held responsible, and not the party who is remotely responsible.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), on the 23rd of November, in the course of his speech, made the following statement:-
In citing these things the point I want to make is that it is very unfortunate that we cannot avoid racial and religious appeals in this country. Should such appeals not he stopped? Is it not the duty of every good citizen of Canada to endeavour to put an end to them? No political party can reap advantage from them. These appeals do not count for much among political partisans, hut the unfortunate part of it is that there are some people in the country whose minds are influenced by them. . . Is it rot time that racial and religious appeals should cease, and that all Canadians should work together for the prosperity and progress of our country?
The Prime Minister, at the conclusion of his speech delivered the day before yesterday, also made a statement and an appeal; the statement being that he had never, in the course of his political life, relied upon appeals to race and creed, and an appeal that such methods of political campaigning should be laid aside in this country. Now, Mr. Speaker, so far as these two statements are concerned, they are correct in the spirit that they embody, they are fine as far as words go, they are absolutely right in theory. But the question that I wish to discuss for a few moments is as to how these hon. gentlemen, and the party to which they belong, and which the Prime Minister has Mr. PERLEY.	,
long led, how this party and these gentlemen have, in their practice, realized these fine theories, these high and perfectly proper ideals. I think we would all be relieved in the Dominion of Canada if we could once and for all put away entirely from the politics of this country all these unworthy and damaging methods of political campaigning. Everybody knows that an appeal to reason, to intelligence and to conscience is the proper one to make. Everybody knows, at least after he has had some experience of public affairs, that that kind of appeal is the only one which, in the end, pays, and that an appeal to prejudice and to ignorance, though it may be temporarily successful, in the end all comes back upon the man or the party that uses it.
I do not deny that temporary advantages may be gained but I do say as a fact that they are but temporary and that whilst they are harmful to the public life of the country, damaging and hindering to the progress and development of the country, they are, in the end, neither useful nor advantageous to the party that uses them.
The statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and the assertion and the appeal made by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, make it necessary to trace for a little the course of these gentlemen in the public annals of the country. I do not propose to go into this matter thoroughly or fully ; if I did it would take more time than I have at my disposal, or than this House could give even for such an object. I propose simply to give a few specimens, culled from 1896 up to the present and to place them side by side with these fine theories and high ideals and to ask the House and the country to decide how practice and theory, performance and ideals, meet, as regards the action and the course of my hon. friends opposite.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in 1896 was a representative in this House and a worker in his party, and I suppose he stood well in the councils of his party. Anyway he has since been selected to fill one of the most responsible positions in the cabinet of the Dominion. In 1896 that hon. gentleman ran a campaign in the province of Quebec. He had been in this House before that time and on the occasion of a vote for money to pay for Lee-Enfield rifles and some field artillery which was absolutely necessary to arm the militia of this country and to bring their armament up to anything like a modern standard he flatly opposed the vote, not only on financial grounds but on the ground that this country had no business, no right, no duty, no obligation to assist in the defence of the coun-

try in so far 'as it took away from the burden of Great Britain. In this House he voiced his dissent from the vote, he voiced his sentiment that that was a matter, if it was to be done at all, for Great Britain to do, and said that he himself was very much surprised that Great Britain who, he understood, was to protect this country and the colonies had asked us to buy and pay for the artillery which was necessary to arm the militia of this country. In that spirit he went to the country and took a prominent part in organizing and carrying out the campaign in the province of Quebec. He assisted in that campaign by his own platform utterances and by writing in the papers supporting his side of politics. He assisted in that campaign by having papers that were devoted to his party voice his own views. I shall read one extract only from ' Le Soir ' of June 18, 1896, as a sample of the statements which were published broadcast and used in the general election of 1896 in the province of Quebec. It reads :
One of the fads of Old Tupper is imperial federation. Imperial federation means a more intimate alliance between England anil her colonies in general and more especi-ially with Canada. One of the conditions of that alliance would be that in time of war, Canada should be called upon to pay a share of its costs both in men and money. And, as England is nearly always at war with some one, we would be forced to continually tax ourselves to find the money and draw lots to furnish the men. And in return, England would make these droll baronets, or knights of this, or commanders of that. But the people will remain food for powder.
Sir Charles Tupper had hardly returned from England than he began to prepare the means for the realization of this awful project.
The article then goes on to summarize the difficulties that England was in, one with the United States over the Venezuelan question. It then mentions my resolution of 1896, of the 21st of April for the amount of money that was required, and continues :
And why should we fight for England?
Why all these warlike preparations if we are not to have war?
The electors should bear in mind that those big and fat leaders who are always desirous to exhibit themselves as more patriotic than others, more loyal than others, and ready to plunge us into war for the benefit of others, will not he the parties who will pay and hear the burden. Those rifles, those guns, the electors will have to handle. You are considered good only for food for the cannons. The Tnppers, the Angers, the Taillons, will be in their offices as ministers, from where they will send you to death with light hearts, and a glass of champagne in their hands. Once more, why all those rifles, guns and bayonets, if this good Tupper and Company do not intend some sinister design? Your
children -will he sent to Africa and Asia whence they will not come back.
And so on and so on. That is in the campaign of 1896. In ' Le Soir ' newspaper which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows very well ; it is said that he contributed to it and I have never heard that he denied.
My hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), is sometimes independent and sometimes not quite so independent. Yesterday he referred to the appeal made in the contest of Drummond and Arthabaska, an almost exact transcript of that just read by me. My hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) said that was damnable language. What does he think of the language which if not actually written by the minister appeared in ' Le Soir,' the organ of the party in full sympathy with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in 1896 which was circulated everywhere through Quebec and brought its toll of votes from the prejudices and feelings aroused and by virtue of which and similar articles the Minister of Marine and Fisheries sits here to-day, by virtue of which and similar utterances my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) is able to say that he sits on the ministerial rather than on the opposition side of the House.
If these were damnable in the Arthabaska-Drummond election, were they not equally damnable in the elections of 1896? But the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is to-day robed in his innocent and more loyal habiliments, and he appeals to us now to have nothing to do with the appeals to race and to religion, and he deprecates the use of such appeals. But, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is not on record in this House, or in this country, or in any part of this country, for ever having lifted his voice to put down such appeals as those which were being circulated, and which brought the grist to his own mill in 1896. Now, Sir, I am going to read another of these, and here it is:-
The most important issue before the electors is the question of imperialism. In the future if you elect a partisan of the Conservative party, of Sir Charles Tupper, Canada will have to contribute to every important war of the empire.
If war were to break out with France or Russia, we would have to send at least one hundred thousand men. Where would they find them?
They would resort to conscription, and I would submit to you ladies here present, that they would come into your homes, carry ofi your husbands, your beloved sons; young girls, they would cary oft your lovers, to fight in a war in which this country had no interest. I am opposed, as I always have been, to any contribution on the part of Canada to any war of the empire, whether

53&
great or small, whether just or unjust.
1 denounce the policy of assisting Great Britain. I still have confidence that the Liberal party can restore the feeling of safety.
The Conservative party is pledged but Sir Wilfrid is not.
Does my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), not recognize in this the very sub-stratum and foundation of the articles that were read by the Minister of Marine as having been used in Drummond-Artha-baska? Is not this also damnable language? By whom was it used and in whose interest was it used? It was used in the election of 1896 and 1900; it was. spread everywhere through the province of Quebec; it was used by a disciple of my right hon. friend, who, having used it so faithfully and to such good effect, has been rewarded by the right hon. gentleman, and is to-day a judge in the province of Quebec, because of his work. Then, my right hsn. friend had a very industrious and able colleague at that time, and that colleague did yeoman's work for him in the province of Quebec and elsewhere :-
England be blowed.
The manifesto of Sir Charles Tupper savours of imperialism. There is the fast Atlantic service, to cost $750,000; the policy of rifles and fortifications, $3,000,000; and" the trans-Pacific cable, which will cost millions!
What is there in all this that is of interest to Canada ?
England has an interest in uniting Australia and Canada by cable, in garnishing our frontiers and our ports with fortifications, and in having rapid steamers between Quebec and Liverpool.
In case of war with other nations England will find these very convenient and very useful.
Have good sense and patriotism.
Work for Canada and for the well-being of her population before sacrificing our efforts for the glorification of England.
French Canadians, be on your guard!
I cite that from ' La Patrie ' of May 6.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
Very well, he became your colleague shortly after and I will give my right hon. friend something that was written in 1990, which is even hotter, and I think I had better give it just now. This was in 1900:-
Mr. Tarte's final appeal to the people of Quebec is published in ' La Patrie ' to-night, and is as follows:	_	,
Patriots vote on Wednesday against the in-sulters of our nationality, against the enemies of our province.
' My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was alive in 1904, and in 1904 there was a newspaper called ' Le Canada.' Now, there aTe newspapers and newspapers in the province of Quebec; some of them are business papers and are run on commercial principles; others are political papers that draw the breath of life and their daily bread from the government of the day. ' Le Canada ' is such a one as that. 'Le Canada,' I believe, had an able lot of writers. It is. said that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself was one of these Vriters, but at all events that paper was no doubt well scanned by the hon. gentleman, and I have no doubt he knew what was going on. Well, Sir, in 1904, whether the conception was that of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or not, whether the mechanical execution was done by the Minister of Marine or not, there appeared in ' Le Canada,' in 1904, just before the elections of that year, a cartoon which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in a moment of forgetfulness, or of extreme audacity, tried to palm off on this House a few days ago as a cartoon conceived, executed and distributed by disloyal Nationalists-and may be by equally disloyal Liberal-Conservatives in the Drum-mond-Arthabaska election. What was the teaching of that cartoon in 1910, according to the words of the hon. gentleman himself? He told us it was criminal and shameful. Was it less criminal and shameful in 1904, on the eve of the elections, when it was published in ' Le Canada,' and was distributed everywhere through the province of Quebec, and, in the interests of whom? In tm interest of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, who made his pious declaration the day before yesterday in this House. Was it shameful and disgraceful in 1904? There is only one thing I know that could be more shameful and disgraceful than that in a party canvass, and that I shall mention a moment later. Should a public man in this country, a Prime Minister of the Dominion, a minister of the cabinet in

this country, profit by what they must have seen day after day under their own eyes and in their own paper; to profit by disgraceful and shameful cartoons, the teaching of which was what? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries was eloquent almost (for him) the other day when he said: I have stood by the British flag, I stand now by the British flag, I shall always stand by the British flag.
Was fie standing for the British flag, was his party paper standing for the British flag, when in 1904, on the eve of an election, it posted up before the electors of the province of Quebec a cartoon which represented Jean Baptiste with both hands holding up the Union Jack, the British flag, and just at one side of him the Briton himself taking advantage of Jean Baptiste's grip upon the British flag to rifle his pockets and steal his money? Is that the way to uphold the British flag? That, it seems to me, is the way to teach, as they unfortunately have taught too many in the province of Quebec, that the British flag is to be viewed with suspicion, and that British power also is to be viewed with suspicion. I said there was only one more infamous than that; what is that one? It is one which at the time was sent to me. I have made diligent search for it; I have been unable to find it. But I have its description, what is it? In the year 1900 there was distributed broadcast in the province of Quebec a cartoon which I will describe. Yonder is a citadel. Inside of it is Laurier and Tarte and others of the Liberal leaders. Behind them is the French population of Quebec. In front comes up a straggling horde of Tories armed to the very teeth, with long streaming banners, and on these banners the inscriptions, ' Down with the Pope,' ' Down with the French Canadians,' ' Down with the Roman Catholics.' I said there was only one baser cartoon that was possible than the one which must be fathered by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; this is the one, Sir. My right hon. friend profited from that appeal to prejudice, an appeal which might have brought votes to him, but which was of a character so debasing, so mean, so utterly mischievous and dangerous in a country like this, that it passes the wit of man to conceive that anybody could have concocted it, let alonft have distributed it amongst the French population of the province of Quebec. My right hon. friend himself was not above an appeal to race prejudice. In the elections he said at St. Lin:
I am a French Canadian like yourselves. The same blood runs through my veins that runs through yours. I foresaw the war that would be waged against me on account of my race and religion. That war has now burst upon me with a bitterness which I little expected. I am attacked in the province of Ontario because I am a French Canadian, and the declaration is repeatedly made that
a French Canadian has no right to be a premier of a British colony.

No, I may not have brought out the worst. Now, Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand a little pamphlet which was published and used in the province of Quebec in the year 1900. It has thirty-eight pages. It is of course printed in French. It is entitled:	' Le Toryism, Voilk.
l'Ennemi.'
Now, I make the statement that from the first page of the thirty-eight in that pamphlet, issued and distributed by the Liberal party as a campaign document in the province of Quebec in 1900, there is not one single question of policy raised. Tariff is not discussed; taxation is .not discussed; trade policy is not discussed; Grand Trunk Pacific is not discussed-was not then in existence; nothing is discussed of all the matters of policy which from 1896 up to that time had divided and were dividing the parties. From the beginning to the end of it there is nothing else than an appeal to the race instincts and the religious instincts of the people of the province of Quebec. I am going to read some of the headings:
(Translation). The importance of the next election cannot be overlooked by any one.
The question to-day is not one of protection or of free trade, having but a material interest; the future of the Canadian nation is at stake.
From the evening of the 23rd of June, 1896, our opponents have resolved to ask the English population of this country to give their suffrages against the cabinet of which Sir Wilfrid Laurier is the head, for the reason that the Prime Minister is a French Cana-adian.
Not some pagers have so demanded, not some individuals have so demanded, but ' nos adversaires out resolu.' I will read this in English for the benefit of my hon. friend from Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) whose early education has been neglected.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
I will read it in French if the hon. member wishes.

Mr# FOSTER (reading):
From the evening of the 23rd of June, 1896, our opponents (that is, the Conservatives of the Dominion) have resolved to ask the English population of this country to give their suffrages against the cabinet of which Sir Wilfrid Laurier is the head, for the reason that the Prime Minister is a French Canadian.

The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and the honour of the empire. *
I say that this clause 4 absolutely binds this parliament and this House, so far as a resolution can bind, to make an emergency contribution to the defence of the empire if there is no other contribution that you have, or, even if you have any other it gives you the right and the liberty to make it. I make this still stronger by what fell from my right hon. friend in his speech the day before yesterday when he said that the leader of the opposition proposed a contribution of $25,000,000 as an emergency contribution, and here are the words of the Prime Minister :-
We knew that there was no emergency and so we voted against the contribution proposed by the opposition.
What does that mean? Does it not mean that they voted against an emergency con-184
tribution because they did not believe there was an emergency, which implies that if the Prime Minister believed there was an emergency he and his party would feel themselves at liberty to vote for an emergency contribution.
Now, I take clause 4 and I say it goes further than that; I say it binds this parliament in a case of emergency, if there is nothing else to be done, to come to the aid of the defence of the empire by monetary contribution. I ask my right hon. friend what he meant when he said, that if vital trouble threatened Great Britain, Canada would rush to the assistance of Great Britain. I put this case to him: Suppose to-day the contingency arose that it became suddenly and certainly known that war was imminent between Germany and Great Britain, suppose it was so stated by the British government; suppose it was made clear to the cognizance of the Prime Minister; suppose that that state of things existed, how does the Prime Minister propose to aid the empire in the terms of clause 4 of that resolution? He has no ships, he has no men; he cannot refuse to do anything because that resolution pledges him to do all that can be done, and the only resource he would now have in his power would be to propose a parliamentary vote in aid of a service in defence of the empire. So I say that clause 2 stops the mouth of the man who says that that resolution of parliament denies an emergency contribution, and I say that clause 4 of the resolution makes it absolutely necessary that you must make a contribution, (if you keep faith with parliament and with that resolution), if you have nothing else to give; or, if having given whatever else you have to give you think the danger so great that still greater resources of Canada should be given for the benefit of the empire, and to protect and maintain us as a part of that empire.
Well, Sir, what are the terms and conditions of that resolution? There is to be a Canadian service. That does not mean, and it did not mean at that time, that a Canadian service to be a Canadian service had to be built in this country; that every ship had to be constructed in Canada, and manned with Canadians. That was not what was meant by a Canadian service. If every vessel were built in the ship yards of Great Britain, under the direct supervision of the admiralty, it would be a Canadian service, and it could be a Canadian service if every man on board of it was an Englishman and not a Canadian. It is to-day, our hon. friends opposite say, a Canadian service, and yet almost every man that you have on board that service is not a Canadian, because we have no Canadians yet who are drilled up and ready to take their places there. If my hon. friend will do me the justice to read my speech he will see

that was what was foreshadowed by me. I said that at first the Canadian service would have to be built in Great Britain, because we had not the facilities to build it here, and that it had to be manned by British officers and sailors until we had educated and prepared- oux own men for that service. That did not make it any the less a Canadian service. Do you mean to say that the Australian unit is not an Australian service because its vessels have been built in Great Britain and have been manned for the most part by British officers and British sailors?
Now, Sir, the terms of that resolution were that you were to establish a speedy Canadian service. Have you made a speedy Canadian service? Two years have passed since then, and show me even the bones of your Canadian service in the line of giving aid to the empire in case of stress and war. Therefore, the term ' speedy ' has not been carried out as it has been carried out by Australia and by New Zealand. But there was more than that:-

Mine was what it is tonight-not that we should simply get to-Mr. FOSTER.
gether a lot of officials and pay their salaries, but that we should have the speedy organization of the service to bring out the service.

speechtext: The speedy commencement.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: Organization is commencement, is it? Well, I leave my hon. friend to his own cogitations, and the public's; both of them will be severe enough, I think. In the second place, this was to be in cooperation with the imperial navy. That was as much a part of the resolution as was the speedy organization of the service. Is this organization going on in cooperation with the imperial navy? Just the opposite. Localization is the distinctive feature of this service as it is proposed. Segregation is a second feature of it. Antagonism is another feature of it, and a very possible one. It is not in co-operation with the imperial navy; it is separate, distinct, segregated, antagonistic to the imperial navy, and it has been shown in this House how it may lead to very grave danger. It was to be in close relation to the imperial navy. Is it? The close bond of connection with the imperial navy has been entirely cut. It is distinct from it. What is proposed is unsuitable to fit in with the British navy. There is no unit to be inter-changable. There is no sufficient body to make an adequate war practice possible, and consequently it is not in close relation to the imperial navy. Again, it was to be along lines sugegsted by the Admiralty in 1907. What were those? I am not^going to quote what was stated by the Admiralty. All this House knows that the lines laid down by the Admiralty in 1907 amongst other things had these two great characteristics: that it was to be under the control of the Admiralty in time of war. My right hon. friend will not deny that, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will not deny that. Read Lord Selborne's memorandum, read every memorandum that has been issued by the Admiralty since, and you will find that they take the ground that the Admiralty, the supreme controlling force must in time of war direct the situation of the vessels and conduct the battle so that victory may be won. Giving up everything else, they declare that they cannot give up that. They are against the localization of navies, and are absolutely in favour of one supreme control in time of war. Is that not a part of the resolution? Has that part been carried out?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: So far as I remember, Lord Tweedmouth never said it.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
Lord Tweedmouth's memorandum says:
We welcome you, and we ask you to take some leading part in making more complete than it is at present the naval defence of the empire. I wish to recognize all that our cousins over the sea have done in consequence of decisions of former conferences. I know that you gave to the government and to the Admiralty, with a free and unstinting hand, the heln that you thought you could manage to give. Gentlemen, I have only one reservation to make, and in making it I ask that, as we have proved ourselves successful in the past, you should put your trust in us now. The only reservation that the Admiralty desire to make is, that they claim to have the charge of these strategical questions which are necessarily involved in naval defence, to hold the command of the naval forces of the country and to arrange the distribution of ships in the best possible manner to resist attack and to defend the empire at large, whether it be our own islands or the dominions beyond the seae. We thoroughly recognize that we are responsible for that defence. We want you to help us in that defence. We want you to give us all the assistance you can, but we do not come to you as beggarswe gladly take all that you can give us, but at the same time, if you are not inclined to give us the help that we hope to have from you, we acknowledge our absolute obligation to defend the King's dominions across the seas to. the best of our ability.
No one but the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the man who has the supreme control and charge of this great service in this country, would have questioned that for a single moment in this House. Well, Sir, I come to another and still more important point. There was the vital fire which warmed this whole resolution, and what was it? It is expressed here, and I will read it:
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy along the lines suggested by the Admiralty at the last imperial conference and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Great Britain is essential to the securitv of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
That was the overruling consideration; that was the vital warmth and fire which made the whole thing living and strong. Have my right hon. friend and his party, in making these proposals and organizing for carrying them out, done it in full sympathy with that view, that it is essential to the commerce and the safety of the empire and the peace of the world that the British imperial fleet shall be supreme? If
they have not, they have failed to carry out that resolution. I know of no nobler form of expression, I know of no nobler and higher sentiment than is contained in these few words: In full sympathy-with what? With the absolute necessity of a British fleet to maintain commerce, to maintain the peace and safety of the empire, and to maintain the peace of the world. See what that means and what it calls for. British commerce encircles the globe. There is not a league of water which is not traversed by some toiler of the sea in the multitudinous and tremendous commerce that is being carried on within the empire and under its aegis. What does that commerce mean? It means the development, the comfort, the progress and the uplifting of the world. That commerce goes into every corner of the globe, bearing with it social, political and national life, the higher civilization, and everything that follows in the wake of great diffusive and peaceful intercourse. When this plan of a Canadian service was originated, that was the dominant idea and that was the great object to be sought by those who originated it. Take the other object, the safety of the empire, what does that mean? An empire which girdles the globe under which innumerable millions of people are enjoying the benefits of British supremacy and depending upon British ad-were exercised at any previous time in the ministration. Mighty trusts, such as never were exercised at any previous time in the world's history, are being worked out by the empire in India, Egypt and other parts of the world. The safety of the empire-contrast that for a single moment with the possible crash and fall of the empire and the chaos into which the world would be plunged by such a calamity. The peace of the world -what does that mean? It means that, under its benign influence, the human race, free from war's alarms blooms and fructifies in every department of life and endeavour, as does nature's growth under the distilled dews, the warm rains, and the grateful heat of summer suns.
That idea is a noble one. No man had the right to endorse the resolution without having his mind embued with sympathy for its great object. That is the reason we parted company with the right hon. gentleman. We stood for that resolution, we stand for it yet, and loyally we abide by it. We do not want a mangled abortion. What we want is the whole resolution carried out on the terms and conditions on which this House declared it should be carried out. What do you propose? You propose a Canadian naval service. Yes, but you deny and violate every one of the conditions that the resolution threw about that service. Your very scheme undermines the spirit and the letter of that resolution. The spirit was broad, effective, patriotic and imperial in its best sense. Your action has been nar-

row, ineffective, unpatriotic, anti-imperial. The resolution recognized what the empire meant to us-our commerce, security and progress. It recognized what the navy meant to the empire-its bulwark and defence and our obligation and privilege to strengthen that bulwark and defence. What strength to bulwark and defence can this proposition give which has been submitted to parliament by the hon. gentlemen opposite? Your service shrivelled into an instrument of minimum use to Canada, practically valueless to the empire-ineffectual, costly and dangerous. By it the defence of the country, the defence of the empire has been obscured by petty and incidental party advantages which are expected to spring from it, by consideration of locality and section, and these smaller considerations which should have no weight in the proper carrying out of the larger scheme. By a process of inversion you have made what should be the first object a secondary one. How different has it been in the other dominions. New Zealand has her Dreadnought already under way. No one hears ny New Zealand such strife as has been raised here and which has humiliated Canada. Australia has been loyal to the spirit of that resolution though she had no hand in framing and passing it. To-day two Australian destroyers built in Britain, are in her own ports, and the third one, made in Great Britain, is now being put together in Australia. And in June, 1912, the Australian unit will be completed and in Australian waters, ready for service for the protection of that colony and the defence of the empire. Let me point this out, that in the whole debate, in all the newspaper controversy in Australia, never has a single voice been raised against the aim, the unity of purpose, the ultimate object of the Australian navy unit. That navy stands by the islands of Australia and patrols her shores in time of peace. In time of war it goes undoubtedly to the defence of the empire. Take South Africa. To-day South Africa, a young country, with immense burdens and small population and revenue, gives a half million dollars per year as her contribution out and out to the defence of the empire and sends it to the British Admiralty for that purpose. There you have the three sister dominions, without quibbling, in a straightforward manner, ranging themselves, not suspiciously, but loyally, and openly by the side of the British government and the imperial power and quickly and heartily providing an adequate contribution to the defence of the empire and their own protection.

I would ask my hon. friend if there is anything in the resolution he has quoted or the speeches in its behalf declaring the advisability of submit-Mr. FOSTER.
ting the Canadian naval programme to the people of Canada?

speechtext: I shall give my hon. friend his answer in the order in which I propose to deal with that point in my remarks.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
When I say that I will answer this question in the order in which it comes , I am quite sure that my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) will agree with me in taking that position and will wait for his answer. I did not at once answer my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. C. A. Wilson), who put a question in the middle of a sentence. But I said I would answer him, and I did answer according to my lights and my convictions.
Now, there are two conceptions of the service that is due from Canada and by Canada. We have the conception of the Minister of Marine. I make bold to say that we could not expect a very high conception of the service due by Canada to the empire from that hon. gentleman. If we consider his participation in the campaign of 1896 we could hardly expect him to have a high conception of the service he was to be instrumental in forming for the Dominion. And, if we take into account his action in 1904 in relation to the cartoon of which mention has been made here, we should expect still less of him. In the conference of 1907, how did he stand? I read last year, when the hon. gentleman was not here, part of a speech made by him in that conference. As he is here now, I desire to read it again. Standing in that conference of 1907, representing Canada before the delegates of the empire and making excuse for lack of past action and for no further action, he spoke these words:-
We have on the Great Lakes (large seas, properly speaking) American states bordering these Great Lakes, and they are having navies of their own now. I think that three states bordering on the three great' lakes, Ohio, Michigan and Illinois are spending not less than $15,000,000 themselves for keeping up a navy on these lakes, and are drilling their men on the shore of the lakes. Besides they have some ships which are not on-because it would be against the conclusions of the treaty-but built in order to be prepared in case of emergency. As far as Canada is concerned, one of the first duties we shall have to look after is our protection in connection with the Great Lakes. I may say that the wars we have had since 1763, since Canada has become part of the British Empire, came from the United States. We had an invasion in 1775, we had an invasion in 1812, and we had the Fenian raids in the 60s. All those invasions came from the United States. So we have to look specially to protect ourselves in that direction, and I may say we have been doing it as far as the Great Lakes are concerned, not to a very large extent it is true, but to the extent of spending a sum of money

which is quite important for a country of i the size of ours.	<
I would like to ask the Minister of Ma- j rine: Did he consider then that he was ( making a truthful representation to the j delegates of the empire? If he did not, why did he make it? If he did, and it was truth- . ful, what has he done since to carry out ' what he said was Canada's duty in protect- ; ing her borders upon the Great Lakes? _ I tell the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that his words were an absolute misrepresentation of Canada's ease before the delegates of the empire-I mean ' misrepresentation ' in the original sense, a representation that is not right. Why did the minister make it? To deceive the empire? Will he stand by his statement now? Will he say that it is the duty of Canada, and has been for two years, to make provision to protect herself on the Great Lakes? Will he say that he has stood by that duty and implemented his own words? The hon. gentleman stands in the face of the empire in relation to that statement much as he stood in the face of this country on that cartoon business of 1904. The delegates of the empire, listening to the words of the Minister of Marine as explaining the position of Canada, could not. possibly come to a right conclusion as to Canada's real position. Was the minister trying to frame an excuse foT Canada? But, if an excuse is to be offered it should at least have some foundation _ in fact-this had no foundation in fact._ Think of a representative of Canada declaring that we cannot do what the representatives of the empire would like us to do, because, forsooth, we have first the duty of defending ourselves on the lakes; that invasions have always come from the United States; that we fear them still; therefore, our first duty is to fortify ourselves along the line of the Great Lakes. Is the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) proud of his colleague who would make a statement like that? Yet, the Prime Minister sat there and heard the statement, and there is no record that he raised his voice to mitigate or modify it. So,
I say, we cannot expect much from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bro-deur). But that hon. gentleman comes down to this House in this year, 1910, and give us reasons why we should have a navy. And what is that reason? He says that Great Britain has withdrawn her ships from Canada, and now there is not a single ship left to protect Canada, and therefore we have to provide for our own protection and defence. Is that a fair statement coming from a Canadian minister and directed against the power of Britain? I Tead to this House and the minister heard it-but he had heard it before in the conference of 1907-that, after all the quibbling and excuses for the determination to do nothing for the empire, Lord Tweedmouth stood forward and said: Do much, or do little, whatever you do, we still acknowledge that the King's dominions are to be protected by us and we propose to do it. Yet the teaching of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, here and in the province of Quebec, is that we are forced to have a fleet because Britain has withdrawn her protection from Canada. And he gives as his second reason why we must have a fleet the statement that we must protect our commerce. Why? Because, he gives us to understand, our commerce is left unprotected by Britain to-day. Both of these statements he made in this House; both of them he made in Quebec; both of them he will continue to make, and both of them are absolutely without foundation. I am surprised, Sir, that a Canadian minister will try to spread that impression in a British country. Does he not know, as you know, Mr. Speaker, that every vessel that floats the English flag, that every vessel within the empire to-day, is under the certain protection of the British fleet? Does the British fleet have to hover about every smack, and every schooner, and every vessel in order to afford it protection? The British fleet has been existent for centuries. It has so permeated this world with its energy, and power, and the watchfulness of the flag, that no matter whether this fleet is in the North Sea or the Mediterranean, commerce everywhere the wide world over is protected by the power and majesty of that fleet. Does the sun have to divide itself up into bits to put a little of its light and heat alongside every planet in the universe, in order to warm the universe? No, Sir, the central sun is there, compact and powerful, in one body, and it strikes with its rays every part of the universe of which it is the centre. What libel more mean, what libel more dastardly, than to try to teach the people here or elsewhere that the British government, has withdrawn its protection from us, therefore we are obliged to have a navy of our own?
But there is one thing that rejoiced the Minister:	It is another proof of our autonomy, and therefore we build a fleet. We organize a fleet in order to prove our autonomy. Why, he says: Now, we can have war vessels of our own, we don't have to ask Great Britain to allow us. We have got our naval autonomy, and this is an evidence of it. There is the conception of my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; I leave it with this House to . say if it is a worthy conception. Oh, but .. there is another. In reply to us on this , side of the House, he denied that he had : signed any document by which the control : of this fleet in time of war should be in the ? British Admiralty. The British govern-[DOT] ment said that he had, the British govern-r ment said that the colonies acknowledged - that. My hon. friend said, I have never

signed the document, it cannot be found. Is that his repudiation of it? So he and the Prime Minister stand together. They say: The needs of the empire have nothing to do with us, we will confine ourselves to Canada. We may come to the aid of the empire in need or we may not; but we hold absolutely to cutting that connection, and acknowledging no bond or tie. That is what both of them said. It is well for us to remember what they say, and to keep it in mind.	'	.
Now what is the Prime Minister's conception? Not much broader. The Prime Minister went down to the city of Montreal to speak to a monster meeting to pave the. way for his instructional campaign in the province of Quebec. There he gave the reason for the formation of the Canadian service. What was it? He said that in 1902 the British government had demanded of him and his colleagues at the conference that they should contribute, that they should recruit, equip and maintain a reserve force.

speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
But I tell you exactly what the impression was, whether it was meant or not. The impression was that Great Britain, in 1902, put it up to Canada that she should recruit and maintain a reserve force always to be at the disposal of the War Office in London, and had put it up to the Canadian delegates that they should contribute an annual sum for the maintenance of the British fleet. Those two things, I have them under my hand, my hon. friend will not deny them. With reference to the first he said to his audience:	There, gentlemen, was the
entrance into the maelstrom of militarism, and that I opposed with all my force. To the second he said:	To
that I gave a categorical refusal. I stood between Canada and the demand of the British government, I stood between Canada and the proposed invasion of the autonomy of Canada. I, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, stood there as your defender. Now, Sir, whatever the word ' demander ' may mean,
I say he would have been frank if he had said: These suggestions were made at the conference, but they were made by delegates at that conference, of which the British government was one; and before those delegates were conferred with at all, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain addressed the conference and said in effect to the assembled delegates:	We call you here to lay
before you the condition of affairs. The

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
empire is wide, its burdens are heavy, we must maintain its defence. We do not come to you as beggars, but we ask you to take these things into consideration, and if you feel that you can in any way help, we ask you to help; but if you don't, we will do it. Recollect, we dont come to demand or to beg. Did my right hon. friend add that in his speech in Montreal? If he had, he would have told the men who were to read it, the hundreds of thousands in Quebec, who were to read it, that all that was asked was proposed by the delegates. At the same time he might have said: My countrymen, 1 must be frank enough to tell you that Great Britain, on the very threshold of that conference, stated to us: We force you in nothing, we do not beg from you, we do not categorically demand, we do not command you to do_ anything. There is the situation, help us if you can; but if you cannot, it lies with yourselves. Does not my right hon. friend think that would have been a truer representation of the case than the one he made? He went on and said: You ask my reasons why we formed a navy. There are two: First, we are richer, and more populous than in 1902 and therefore we are better able to support a navy. Secondly, since 1902 we have become a nation, and all great nations must prepare for their own defence. There he stopped. The imperial idea never seemed to have entered his brain. If it did, he smothered it there, and he put forth what I have stated as the sole reason for a Canadian navy. That representation would have been much more true if he had said something in sympathy with that navy upon which the British Empire, and the commerce, and the peace of the world depend, which was, as I said before, the vital point.
Well, Sir, let me hurry on. I will not follow, as I had designed to do, my hon. friend in some of his arguments. But there is one thing I think I may fairly say. Judging from the speech of my hon. friend the day before yesterday, judging from his statement in 1909 when he declared that he stood absolutely by the position of 1902, judging from the memorandum of 1902, the Prime Minister, so far as he goes, holds to this and this -alone : A Canadian naval service, built in Canada, manned by Canadians, confined absolutely to Canada. Now as then, he stands by the policy of 1902 : We may allow that fleet to aid Great Britain if we consider Great Britain's war is just and that we ought to help. Could not France do the same, could not Russia do the same, could not any country under an absolutely different form of government do the same? There is where my hon. friend's policy puts Canada not a part of the empire, but standing outside the empire, absolutely indepencf ent ; folding his arms he says just as

France or Italy or Germany even would say, when war arises, we will help Great Britain or we will not as we see fit. But he had informed the House and the country again and again that in the past there had been wars, in which, if he had a fleet and had been premier, he would not have allowed that fleet to take part, he had informed us, he had informed Great Britain and her enemies as well, that in any war that took place where the supremacy of Great Britain was at stake, one of the great overseas dominions had pledged herself that she would not rush into battle for the British Empire. That is the position of my right hon. friend. What does he rest it on? On the cry of autonomy and he quarrelled with me because I stated at one time that I thought that word was overworked-and I say yet I think it is overworked. What do all his fine sentiments about what responsible government had done for Canada, for Australia, for New Zealand and South Africa to do with the present occasion? He declared that responsible government and autonomy was the basis of the empire as well as the foundation of the development and success of all these overseas dominions. Did any one deny it? Does any one doubt it? Who denies autonomy to Canada to-day? Where is it threatened? My right hon. friend is like a belated knight who, after the battle is all over, the victory won and the results gathered in comes with all his fine trappings upon the field of battle and finding no enemy to fight still goes through all the motions, sets his lance at rest, digs his spurs into his charger's side, makes his passes, flourishes his sword, rushes upon an imaginary enemy and then straightening himself up on horseback, rides off and cries : What a champion I am, what a victory I have won. Does my right hon. friend pay the small compliment to the other overseas dominions that they are any less loyal to the rights and to the autonomy of their country than he is? Will he say that Australians have not as keen an appreciation of responsible government as we have, that New Zealanders, that his friend Botha in South Africa, the leader of the National, that is the Boer forces, and the leader of the Dutch party to-day in South Africa-that he is not as keen on defending the rights of his country as Canada is or could be. Well, New Zealand has paid her money and built her Dreadnought, pretty nearly. Australia has pledged her money and has built part and is building the rest of her unit, and Botha himself has forwarded to the British Admiralty his contribution of $500,000 towards the maintenance of a British navy. Not a word of autonomy, no suspicion of England. My right hon. friend is doing
what? Sowing the seeds of suspicion against Great Britain.

speechtext: No, no! Hear, hear!	.

speechtext:
Sowing the seeds of suspicion against Great Britain. His other teaching has brought fruit in the young disciples who have turned his own weapons against him. He is commencing now-no not commencing, he has been doing it for years, to teach the men of Canada; beware of Great Britain, your autonomous rights are in danger, beware, beware, do not let us have anything in common with the empire, it is not to be trusted ; our sister colonies, our mother land, keep on guard against them. That is the teaching of the right hon. gentleman from first to last. It is bad teaching, it will produce bad fruit. My right hon. friend may think he has something to gain from it, I do not think he has.
Now I come to my last point. The right hon. gentleman said : Let us come now to rock bottom. His rock bottom did not go very low, it consisted in trying to extract a ray of sunshine out of a dish of cucumbers that the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) had placed before him. He was not very successful in extracting the sunshine.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
He said : Let us go to rock bottom. Let us ask ourselves as a parliament here to-night/ what is the use, what are we getting, what are we to have? My right hon., friend and his Minister of Marine and Fisheries, for my right hon friend stood right by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in that respect, said in so many words : Great Britain put it up to us to undertake our own defence and relieve the British taxpayer of that burden, and that we have to do and propose to do. That was in his speech on Thursday. That carries out exactly the teaching of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. You are teaching the people of Canada that Great Britain has refused and that her taxpayers have refused to aid in the defence of Canada and that, therefore, we are now bound to take that up. No other meaning can be taken from the words, they were not qualified in the least. What does my right hon. friend then undertake? He undertakes to protect the Dominion of Canada in its commerce on the seas, on its coast line, in its affairs everywhere ; this government proposes to furnish the defence and I suppose adequate defence. My hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) the other night said he would like to see the member for Vancouver or any member

from this side go over to British Columbia and have a few questions put to him. I would like to go over to British Columbia and after the questions had been put to me or before, to put just one single question to British Columbia in this wise : British Columbia a mighty province, rich beyond our estimation or powers of estimation, sparsely populated, out on the far Pacific coast, with your commerce looking Bacificward, yonder beyond are the Chinese, a vast mass of old eastern people awakening to life, there are the Japanese crowding out from their borders, ready to overflow, and on the testimony of the Prime Minister probably going to overflow soon upon the shores of British Columbia. And, my question to British Columbians would be this: British Columbians, in whom, under these circumstances would you rather place your trust-in the British fleet or in the Rainbow; in the declaration of Lord Tweedmouth on behalf of the British government, that their fleet was there to protect the dominions the wide-world over, or, take Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier and say: Oh, we are with you; away with the British fleet, we will take Sir Wilfrid Laurier's promise of protection and we will sleep sound in our beds under the service he proposes. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said two things the other night; first, he declared there was no danger on the east. That is what we always said. If there is no danger on the east we need nothing to protect us there, or, if we are fully protected against danger from the east by other considerations why do you divide the small fleet that you propose and place more than one-half of it on the eastern side of Canada, when in the same breath you declare that all the danger is in the west? I would be recreant to my duty he said if I did not point out there is a danger in the west from the Japanese, from the possible China of a decade to come, may be from Russia. May I ask my right hon. friend how he proposes-leaving Great Britain out of account as he has done-to make provision for protection against that danger? Does he not know that a false security is worse than none? Does he believe that his divided portion of the fleet (consisting when it is all built of one or two or three vessels and not a single one of them a fighting vessel), is adequate protection for British Columbia against eastern peril. Does he? Does he or does the country think for a moment of what it means when,-Britain having been relegated to one side and scouted Tor her protection,-he and his Minister of Marine propose to provide the protection that Canada needs in these perilous times and the perilous times of the future. Could you protect your western coasts by your militia, if Japan were ever Mr. FOSTER.
tb declare war? Do you not know my right hon. friend and does not this House know that the only protection for the western coasts against that peril is a sea-wall in the shape of a fleet? If that sea-wall in the shape of a fleet is not there, 100,000 or 200,000 armed, seasoned warriors, the best in the world, could be landed on our western shores, and our poor militia-well as they would fight and brave as they undoubtedly are-would be swept like autumn leaves before the wind. Is your fleet, my right hon. friend, a sufficient sea-wall? Do you know the fleet that Japan has? Are we secure against the threatened peril unless our fleet is at least equal to the fleet of Japan? Do you propose to make it equal? Do you know what it will cost if you attempt to make it equal? Sir, Canada is not sufficiently protected if you simply protect it against this possible western enemy. You have to protect against any possible combination, you have to protect against the United States as well. May war never take place between two nations that have so much in common, but history has proven over and over again that community of race and community of language and community of trade is no bar against the angry sudden passions that result in destructive and bloody war. Nor is civilization. There was civilization in Germany and France in 1870, the highest grade of civilization, and yet in a moment war broke out, devastating, bloody and costly. If Canada is to be protected by herself you have to face providing adequate protection by sea and adequate protection bv land as well.
Now, Sir, as against that I say there is a better way. What is that better way? It is to trust the British Empire. It is_ to rely on the empire fleet; it is to furnish our part of that fleet according to our means; it is to co-operate with it for home protection and for empire protection as well. Here we have the greatest, mightiest fleet in the world, almost double that of the two next greatest naval nations, ready to defend every foot of the empire's soil, and yet,-think of the absurdity of it- men in Canada like the Minister of Marine, will arise and sav:	that is not for
us; it does not protect us, and then throw it absolutely to one side and say: let us go in for our own adequate protection. Sir, I say, trust the empire, rely on the empire fleet, furnish our own part of that fleet according to our ability. You may rest assured that the British Empire will not ask for an overburdening part. They have not asked for a single ship, they have not asked for a single man, they have not asked for a single penny, and as Lord Rosebery said, they will not until the last man and the last penny is gone. What rhyme or reason is there in a disconnected two-parts protection in this country? Australia has its protection when its unit is built

and it lies on its shores, (except in time of war), protected even from these North Borneo pirates that the Minister of Marine fears; but in time of war the Australian fleet becomes part of the empire's fleet. Times of war are not frequent. When has the empire's fleet been last called out to match itself against the fleet of any other great power? Not since the Crimean war. Periods of war are temporary and occasional and periods of peace are long and continuous. In the periods of peace Australia's unit will gladden the eyes of Australia within her own waters and in times of peace, the contribution of Canada if made in that way, would gladden the sight of Canadians in Canadian waters. But, when the battle is set and the challenge made, and the security of the empire threatened, then the Canadian fleet and the Australian fleet would be there where the battle is fought and not back in the harbours and rivers of the overseas dominions waiting to see what was going to happen.
On these grounds, Sir, I propose to vote for the amendment proposed by my hon. friend. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) asked me whether in my speech there was any suggestion of submitting this thing to the people before any action was taken. To the best of my knowledge, that question was not dealt with by me in that speech; I do not recollect it. I could not be positive; I might have alluded to it; but I certainly did not make a feature of it. Neither was it alluded to by any man in this parliament when the resolution of 1909 was passed. Why net? Because the 1909 resolution was a resolution which indicated Canada's contribution, in as speedy a way as possible, in the emergency which at that time we believed existed; and, Sir, if my right hon. friend and his government had done as Australia did, loyally carried out the spirit of that resolution in relation to, in co-operation with, according to the lines suggested by, the admiralty, and in full sympathy with the idea of the fleet as the bulwark of the safety of the empire, of commerce, and of the peace of the world, this parliament would have had no such question before it as is before it to-night. .Why have we this question? Because the right hon. gentleman cho'se to violate every term and condition of that resolution, and undertook to put in place of what was contemplated in that speech as a contribution to the strength of the empire, a dilatory, ineffective, costly and useless piece of machinery. And it is because he persists in doing that, and that we are not able in this House to induce him to do otherwise, that we appeal, as every constitutional party has to appeal, to the people.
My right hon. friend used an argument in his speech which elicited tremendous applause from his followers. They seemed to
think it was a great argument. Addressing himself to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), he said:
If my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier were convinced that this policy is the first step to conscription, that it is going to tear children from their mothers and is going to send Canadians upon all the seas of the world, to be disembowelled by a German shell, or killed by a Russian bullet or Japanese shot, would his proposal be simply to refer such a monstrous policy to the people? No, he would say: Down with such a policy!-we will oppose it; we will never submit to it. If the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Bor" den) were satisfied, as he has alleged on the floor of this House, and as his friends have alleged here and elsewhere, that this policy is not only ill-advised, but that it is dangerous, that it is a step leading to separation, would he and his friends be content to send that question to the people to pronounce upon it? Would not they denounce and oppose such a policy.
Mr. Speaker, do you take in that argument? It does seem to me that if in a school debate a fourth-form boy were to use an argument of that kind, his leader would give him a complete woolling for it. The leader of the oppostion must not move to refer a thing to the people if he thinks it bad. What he is to do is to get up and say:	'We will have none of it; out with
it.' When.the right hon. leader of the government, with a big majority at his back, says, ' We will have all of it, in with it, on with it,' what is left to the leader of the opposition to do? To appeal to his master and your master and the master of all of us. The right hon. gentleman proposes that we, being opposed to this thing, shall say, ' We will have none of it, out with it, down with it.' My right hon. friend must be a revolutionist . It is only by a revolution that you can correct things in that way. But we are living under a constitutional government; we have constitutional practice; and under constitutional government, the only alternative left to an opposition, when it puts its views strongly before the government and they are voted down, is to say, appeal to the people and let them decide. Will my right hon. friend do it? I do not know, or rather I think I do know. He will not now. He will have to later. Let me tell my right hon. friend that this question is not settled by this vote to-night. It is not settled by the arguments pro and con here; it is not settled even by the Drummond and Arthabaska election, though that is a good pointer; but it has to be settled by the people at large, and I now say to my right hon. friend, when you propose an abortion like this, when you propose an inefficient, costly, useless organization, without a unit, without a fighting vessel, with a divided force upon the two sides of this continent, to cost more in first cost and more in keep than a complete unit would

have cost-when you propose that, you have to justify, it before the people of Canada. All we can do is to try to argue with you, and if you will not submit to the arguments, which are irrefragable and convincing, and if hon. gentlemen do not propose to break their ranks-they have reasons for that-if you will not give way to argument here and now, the time will come when you will give way to argument upon the electoral hustings of this country. I say to my right hon. friend, if you have the courage of your convictions, if you want to get the people's voice upon this matter, if you think your plan is the best and the people will stand by it, there is one way by which you can find out. To-day we are in confusion.

If my right hon. friend desires to settle all this confusion into which he has plunged this country, if he desires^ to settle that confusion which is found in his own ranks, there is a simple way by which he can do it and that is: Vote this amendment, take your supplies, and then dissolve this parliament and appeal to the people.
