colts. And it is such a paper that is distributed in the colleges, and in the convents; for it is a fact that 'Le Devoir' has access to colleges and convents. It is a shame that those who are entrusted with educating our children and bringing them up properly should allow them to read that paper.
That paper states that Mr. Lafortune was elected as an independent, but that Mr. Laurier's whip brought him into line. I an independent! when for thirty years back I have been fighting the battles of the party, to brand me as an independent! No, I am not of such a stamp, and I would not play the hypocrite for the sake of getting the Conservative vote. I stated to the Conservatives in Montcalm: When you vote for D. A. Lafortune, you vote for a Liberal. If you defeat me, you will be defeating a Liberal. Those are the colours under which I entered this House, and I shall leave it flying those same colours.
The member for Hochelaga, my good friend (Mr. Rivet), was present at a large meeting at Rawdon. He ventured to insinuate that the fight was between a government supporter and an independent candidate. I stopped him right there, and as a gentleman that he is, he took it back, saying:	I took him for an independent, he
said, but I see he is more of a Liberal than I am myself.
In the course of this debate, Sir, reference has been made to many things which occurred during the campaign in Drummond and Arthabaska. Now, do you know what these gentlemen have done? They had special constables sworn in whom they had sent to Drummond and Arthabaska for the purpose ostensibly of maintaining order, while in fact they were employed as enumerators. These men visited the homes of the people, inquiring how many children, how many boys there were in the family. That occurred three or four days before polling day. They applied to the clerk of the court where I have the honour to be the representative of the Crown and had these men sworn in to carry on that dirty work. I would like to see these people contradict me. They will continue insulting me in their paper, but that does not affect me, the mud slinging will fall back into their faces.
Mr. Bourassa writes things without realizing their meaning. I read through the desperate article he wrote on polling day.
I was sorry to find what insulting terms he used therein in reference to the Prime Minister. You know, Sir, how he wound up that article: The great man's glory sinks in the. . . .dirt. If it were not for the presence of ladies in the gallery, I would mention the exact word. Well let the ladies close their ears, I shall say the word: The great man's glory sinks 'in dung. How beautiful. And such things will be given Mr. LAFORTUNE.
to read to young girls, college boys, in priests' houses, in respectable homes in Montreal. It is high time a stop be put to it, or else people will think the man is losing his head.
I admit that in the heat of debate, as stated by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, a moment ago, one may lose his temper and say things which should not be said; but when a man goes to the length of signing such stuff, it is no wonder that people should become anxious over his future doings. And by the way what has become of him?
He claims that members do not vote independently ; that they are after patronage. Mr. Lafortune is seeking a judgeship; so is Mr. Ethier. We are trying to get some kind of appointment. Now, what do you think he would do, if only he had the chance? Did he not endeavour to be appointed Speaker of this House? He did. When did he begin waging war on his oldtime leader? Now, if 1 had a word of reproach to say to the Prime Minister, it would be this: You have been too generous towards him, that is how he proposes to repay you presently.
And while we are dealing with office seekers, I may state that there is not a single family in the Dominion which has benefited by so many appointments: judgeships, prothonotaryships, clerkships, positions of deputy clerks, surveyors, assistant engineers, and what not? There is not a single family which has been so much taken care of as his own. And he speaks of office seekers. Well, he should try and gobble up the whole pudding and that would settle the business.
When questioned as to what he did with the money he received from the government when a member of that international commission, he is content with answering: That is none of your business. He never would settle that account. He denounces dishonesty, patronage seekers, boodlers and the like. He should have enough fairness to let us know how he spent that money. But he refuses to give any information as to that.
If we are to believe him, he is the champion and has the monopoly of honesty, honour, devotedness and disinterestedness. Everything in his make up is abnegation. What was the price paid for his treason? Why has he abandoned the Liberal party? What amount, or what kind of reward did he get? Several secret meetings have taken place between himself and the Conservatives. The price to be paid for his cooperation was discussed; the question of the ways and means to be adopted and of the policy to be followed was a matter of debate. In the first place, he said, I lay down this condition, that I shall have a newspaper, of which I shall be the chief editor, and my salary must be $5,000. How

disinterested! Now sliould I be mistaken as" to the exact figure, I pray the representative of ' Le Devoir ' to state the price in to-morrow's issue. That is the kind of disinterestedness you will find in that man. First a newspaper in his own name, then the editorship of that paper with $5,000 of a salary, which, as I am told, was exacted even previous to the issuing of the paper. Such is his disinterestedness. And it is that man who calls us office seekers. As for him, he works solely for the love of God. That is his contention, but who will take stock in such a statement?
There is no end to his harassing and slandering the right lion, gentleman. Why? Would you like to know? I will tell you: he wished to occupy the speaker's chair, which, Sir, you occupy so worthily. In this he failed, and since then he is in a rage and insults everybody. But he will never get there.
At the outset, Mr. Bourassa opened fire on those who were in office in Quebec. He called Mr. Prevost a thief, a boodler, a perjurer, as well as Mr. Turgeon, while still proclaiming his deep admiration for Mr. Laurier. As regards the latter gentleman, he had not a word to say, only praise to lavish on him. He wished to play a part in Quebec, and with that in view, he resigned his seat here to run for the local house in Quebec. He made a stand against Mr. Turgeon, but we defeated him in Belle-chasse by over 800 of a majority. Later on, he was elected accidentally in St. Hyacin-the, though actually defeated by 40 or 50 votes, a deputy returning officer having omitted to initial the bulletins, these had to be put aside. That is how his election came about by one vote. In St. James Division, Mr. Gouin felt so sure of victory, that he did not look after his candidature in that division, running at the same time in Port-neuf where he was elected by an overwhelming majority. Mr. Bourassa, as representative of St. James, proceeded to Quebec, intended on annihilating his opponents. He was bound to prove that Mr. Turgeon and ' Brainless John,' as he then called Mr. Prevost, were thieves. Having failed to do so, he now is making preparations to come back to Ottawa. It appears he intends to run for the Dominion House. However, he has not got there yet; there is something in store for him if he tries. He would revile and slander us, and keep on saying that the right hon. gentleman is about" to go down in the mud.
He proceeded to Belgium to get evidence in support of his charges against Mr. Turgeon, incontrovertible evidence.^ People expected that he would succeed in procuring such evidence in Belgium and that he would-you know how cocksure he always is-reduce Mr. Turgeon to atoms. Now he failed to produce one tittle of evidence in support of his slanderous charges. Did he
not brand Mr. Prevost a perjurer, did he not point out to him as a counterfeiter and a thief? He even insinuated that Mr. Prevost travelled in company with young lady secretaries. He did not dare say so in plain words, he only insinuated immoral conduct on his part. To-day he is cheek by jowl with that same Mr. Jean Prevost whom he slandered and reviled formerly. They are both of a kind. I believe Mr. Prevost is an honest man, as for the other he is a public liar. He insinuated in Bellechasse that he had the support of Mr. Laurier. He spoke in that sense in every locality, so much so that our friends did not know what to think of it. A telegram was sent to the Prime Minister who wired at once that Mr. Turgeon had the full support of the Liberal party. Mr. Bourassa had given to understand that he had the moral support of the Prime Minister. He did not even stop at that. He stated that if he had so wished, he would have Ion" a"o become a member of Mr. Laurier s cabinet He made a similar statement m regard to Mr. Gouin, but was emphatically contradicted. There is nothing beyond that gentleman's reach; any vagary of his imagination at once assumes for him an air of reality. Can you understand such a make up? I for one, am unable to do so. His wrath, his fits of passion, his thirst for vengeance are the result of his failure to reach his ends. He will never forgive the Prime Minister for having preferred to him the Hon. Mr. Brodeur and the Hon. Mr. Lemieux. That meant his utter downfall. What! Prefer Brodeur and Lemieux to Henri Bourassa! Why that is shameful, incredible, preposterous. And from then on, you may be sure that he made it rough for the Prime Minister and all the rest of us; you may be sure that he made things uncomfortable for us.
At Farham he said: I am a Liberal, that is the way he would fly the Liberal colours in order to deceive the people and mislead the youth of the country. He is an envious and jealous fellow. Envy is a combination of jealousy and sorrow brought about by the discovery of the other fellow s superiority. It is a painful feeling, an rritating pain, a feeling both of hatred md anxiety at witnessing the happiness, he success, the welfare enjoyed by others. Snvy, like a flame, blackens whatever lasses overhead and which it cannot destroy. Envy is inspired by egotism, by selfish aims, by offended conceit. Envy, oeing unable to rise to the level of worth, mdeavours to get even by dragging down its rivals. Such is the man, you cannot fail to recognize him.
Our opponents propose that we have recourse to a plebiscite, in order to find out whether the government should incur that expenditure on the navy. Why did they not make the suggestion at the time the

resolution was introduced on March 29, 1909. Was a plebiscite resorted to at the time confederation was established? Not at all, the word was not yet known at the time. Was there a plebiscite suggested in connection with the Northwest Territories, or in connection with the Pacific scandal, or the canals, or the school question over which you have been weeping for so long? Did you suggest a plebiscite in connection with the Tay canal, with the famous Curran bridge, or with the Connolly-Me-Greevy scandal ? Did you suggest a plebiscite in connection with the traitors' nest which was exposed by Sir Mackenzie Bowell, or in _ connection with the altering of electoral lists and the gerrymandering of constituencies?
On the_ other hand, we have insisted on a plebiscite in 1896, and we licked and defeated you;^ and in 1900, 1904 and 1908 as well. And if Mr. Laurier bids us to defeat you all in 1912, we shall do so. Take care what answer the plebiscite gives you in
In the speech from the Throne, there is a reference to a treaty of reciprocity with the United States. I represent a thoroughly agricultural constituency, and I would rejoice in the interest of my electors to see such a treaty negotiated, if as a result duties were reduced on our exports of farm products. The exportation of hay especially would be greatly benefited thereby.
On the other hand I would feel gratified if our government would do something in favour of the exposition which is to be held in Montreal, and I suggest that a handsome amount be voted towards that end.
Then, I would like that something be done towards the building of the Georgian Bay canal.^ 1 trust the government will consider it their duty to ask the House for a vote in this connection. I hope the government will take the question up in the near future and that we shall be called upon to discuss it in the course of this session.
The member for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel) referred to gifts, to the presentation of an automobile to the Prime Minister. Let me say to the member for Terrebonne that such references are mean in themselves. I know a good many who would not be as generous as the right hon. gentleman, who protects even opponents of his. That is how he is repaid for it. That is the treatment meted out to him. Refrain from referring to such things, and you will have a better name for generosity.
Mr. Tarte's name has also been mentioned. That man never sailed under false colours. He did fight at times with us, but it would have been more becoming on the part of the member for Terrebonne not to recall his memory. You have no respect for the living, but you should at least abstain from reviling the dead.
The name of Mr. Borden, leader of the Mr. LA FORTUNE.
opposition, has been mentioned. The member for_ Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) deprecates his policy; but as I say this, I notice he smiles, which goes to show that he is not very much in earnest. He also deprecates the policy advocated by my own party. He thinks there is something funny in that, since he laughs. But nobody will be deceived by the member for Jacques Cartier. It is hoped that with Mr. Monk as leader of the party in Quebec, and Mr. Borden as leader of the same party in the other provinces, it will be an easy matter to overthrow the Prime Minister. But you are not the stuff to defeat him. How could such a policy be defined? You sound one note here to-day and to-morrow it will be quite another tune. And do you know what is the explanation? These gentlemen term that ' going through evolutions.' These gentlemen are performing evolutions, but their object is always to defeat Laurier.
Reference has been made to fanaticism. What did the late chief of the Conservative party do, I mean Tupper? Did he not say, one day, during the election of 1896 in Regina: 'How could you prefer a French Canadian such as Laurier to one who is English like yourselves? ' And later, when he came down to Montreal and these words were brought home to him, he also 'evolved.' I was speaking in a large hall, he said, and tiles on the roof not being very firmly set, there was some noise in the hall, and I was misunderstood.
On June 22, 1896, Laurier appealed to his fellow citizens of the province of Quebec to only return one of his candidates out of two and that it would be sufficient to make him Prime Minister of Canada. He was not aware that the cry of warning had had its effect and that the French Canadians were about to feply in proper fashion to the fanatical appeal which I have just mentioned by throwing in the face of Tupper a majority of 30 in favour of Laurier. wnen-ever a disposition is shown to run down people of the province of Quebec, you will find us ready to resent aspersions.
Mr. Speaker, I beg your pardon for having spoken at such length, but I judyed tnat it was incumbent on me to vindicate myself and to show in their true light tnose who write such insults and obloquy as I have mentioned. I have a request to make to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier who is my representative, since I have a vote in his constituency: Why do you not put a stop to the insults printed in that newspaper? Why do you allow one of your fellow citizens to be reviled in such a way?
I protest against these infamous sayings published in ' Le Devoir '; it is incumbent on you to protect us. If you do not do so, I say you are not acting right.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, allow' me to beseech the indulgence of the

House so that I may find it an easier matter to get through my maiden speech. My intention is to be courteous towards all, to utter only loyal words as regards Canada and the empire. At the same time I do not wish to deviate from the stand taken during the campaign, or to break faith with those who returned me.
I was selected as candidate, I agreed tq run, and was returned for Drummond and Arthabaska as a protest against the refusal of the government to grant a plebiscite, to protest also against the refusal of the government to take heed of petitions forwarded by the people, and especially from the people of Drummond and Arthabaska.
In Drummand and Arthabaska, we love our country, and we believe that in regard to a question of such importance as that of the navy-a new departure-the people should be consulted. In the county of Drummond and Arthabaska, we have full faith in the wisdom of the province of Quebec as well as in the wisdom of the province of Ontario and of every province in the Dominion. When we suggest that an appeal be made to the people, we do so as regards all the provinces in the Dominion, in behalf of all those living on Canadian soil. We are opposed to the Naval Bill believing that there is in the provisions of that Bill certain things inimical to our autonomy. In the county of Drummond and Arthabaska, we are anxious to preserve that autonomy which has been secured to us through the efforts of all our public men since confederation; we are anxious to preserve it for the benefit of all those who live in the land, for the benefit of Frenchspeaking Canadians, as well as for the benefit of English-speaking Canadians, in a word for the benefit of all those who breathe Canadian air.
In Drummond and Arthabaska, we are anxious to develop the resources of the country, we are anxious that things be so arranged that the Canadian people may have a fair return for any expenditure they make. Let us suppose I am the owner of some property and I put some one on the property to develop it and take care of it. Well, all I can require that man to do is to prevent any trespassing on that property and to enjoy any returns he gets from it. As long as I am confident that he is ready to defend it at the price of his life, I cannot exact any more from him. It is in such manner that I propose fulfilling my duty towards Canada.
When selected to run in that election, the farmers in the constituency were among those who requested me to accept the candidature, so that the farming community might have one more representative in this Parliament. I appealed to the farmers for their vote; when in sympathy with the farming community, one may boast of being in sympathy with all classes of society, for
on that class rests the welfare of the country as a whole.
I was returned to protest against the Naval Bill and to declare in favour of an appeal to the people.
Such was the position I took during the campaign. I have explained it to the electors as they wanted me to do. I wished to be the people's servant. During the campaign I said I was a Liberal. In fact, I am a Liberal, but I do not consider myself bound to- this party such as the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafor-tune) claims to be. He is a lawyer. I was twenty-one years old and I did not know how to write, but I understand that a Liberal is a free man, and I will have lost everything on the day I will have no right to think, to believe or to act.
I will vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) because I think it is more generous and would allow Canadian people to give their own opinion on this Naval Bill and militia question.
Hon. Mr. FISHER (Minister of Agriculture. (Translation.) Before going over the subject now in discussion, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Gilbert) for his maiden speech to-day in this House. I do not approve of his politics on which he has just pronounced himself, nor do I share his views on the subject, but being myself an old member of this House, I wish him personally a hearty welcome.
I would not have undertaken to speak at this late stage of the debate were it not that there are one or two things in the speech of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) which deserve some notice, and ought to be corrected. Before, however, dealing with those matters, I wish to draw attention to the reference which he made to a pamphlet published in the Drummond-Arthabaska election, and which, if I remember rightly, was said to have been published by Liberals. When speaking a few minutes ago the hon. member referred to a certain journal called ' La Gazette d'Arthabaska ' as a Liberal newspaper.
No, I said I thought it was an independent paper.

My information is that the pamphlet was printed in the office of that newspaper, and that, perhaps, is the foundation of the statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite that this pamphlet was put out by Liberals in that contest.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier referred to his dispute, if I may call it such, with the Prime Minister in regard to the passage of a certain order in council. I will not go over the subject, as it has been dealt with by the Prime Minister himself. But if my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has

accomplished anything he has shown the House that the said order in council was passed on the 10th of February, that an order for a return was passed on the 22nd of February, and that the return came down and was made public, and within the knowledge of the hon. gentleman, on the 5th of March. Now, in the earlier part of this debate, the hon. gentleman said that this fact was not made public until long after. We find, however, that the ' long after ' is 25 days, between the 10th of February, when the order in council was passed, and the 5th of March following. One would have supposed, in hearing the hon. gentleman, that months had passed, that a long time had passed. But we find, as a matter of fact, that the publication of that order in council was made just as soon as, in the ordinary routine, it could have reasonably been made. But the hon. member is making a direct accusation of what is not fair, or just, or right ^gainst the Prime Minister. He accuses the Prime Minister of having deceived the people by suppressing certain information-and to that I will refer a little later. But he goes on in regard to this particular occurrence, and states that this order in council was passed during a session of parliament, and that it ought to have been made public and that parliament ought to have acted upon it. My hon. friend knows very well, if he knows anything of constitutional government, that the passage of such an order in council is an act of the executive, that the executive takes full responsibility thereof, and is responsible to parliament for any action arising out of it.
But what is that document, and in what way did it commit this country? It was a despatch in answer to a communication from the imperial authorities, and that communication was a consequence of the imperial conference at which certain conclusions were reached. The action of that imperial conference is well known It took place two years before, and this was but the necessary sequence to the resolutions and conclusions of that conference. The hon. member says that the order in council settled the matter-I took down his words-' The order in council settled the matter.' Now, Mr. Speaker, if that order in council implied any action on the part of the Dominion of Canada, it implied action which must necessarily be carried out by a vote of this House of Commons, by the expenditure of public money, which no order in council could accomplish, but which could only be accomplished after the House had voted the necessary supply to carry that action through. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that any action in regard to the general staff, any arrangement by which the Militia Department of this Dominion could accomplisn what was outlined in that order, must be carried out after the necessary subventions had been Mr. FISHER.
voted, after parliament had discussed the question and had taken action thereupon.

If my hon. friend will allow me-does my hon. friend say that an order in council could bind the country to share in the expense of the maintenance of the general staff, particularly when parliament was in session?
I mean to say that the order in council would not bind; I said that.
Was it a proper matter to deal with by order in council?
Certainly. The hon. gentleman must know that council discusses these matters.	-
It cannot pledge the credit jf the country.
That is just what I am saying, it cannot pledge the credit of the country.
But it did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
That was the view of the Prime Minister, that was the representation of the representatives of Canada.
Would the minister state why the proposals of the War Office were not placed before parliament for discussion and approval?
They are, and they were. They were brought down within 25 days of the date of the action.
After the action?
Certainly.
Why not before?

It was a mere continuance of a principle laid down years before, a principle which had been known to the public at large, and this was only a detail of which the executive took the control and responsibility, and within a few weeks the information was given to parliament. Why did not the hon. gentleman when the information was laid before parliament, if he objects to it, get up and move a resolution of censure on the government?

Is my hon. friend joking? Does he suppose a member of parliament
saw this return? He knows that return was never used or handled until it went to the printer and was half printed. I did not say it was not laid on the table, I said no one saw it until it whs partly printed.

My hon. friend is an old member. He knows perfectly well that every member of parliament has access to every return laid on the table. He now knows, if he did not know before, and I am willing to give him the credit that he did not know, that he spoke without proper information, when he accused my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) of misrepresentation.
I did not accuse the Prime Minister of misrepresentation. I said he had not proceeded in the proper way to lay this matter before the proper authority.

Oh, no, he accused him of misrepresentation and deception of the people of the country. That is the gravamen of his offence, and he appears to have done that without knowledge of the fact that this information was before the public; yet he is the member for Jacques Cartier, an old and experienced member of the House, having had a return laid on the table, he now says that because he did not know it had been printed, he did not know anything about it.
I shall quote one or two words from the second part of the despatch, where I find:
This important question (of the principle of colonial self-government) appears to be adequately provided for in the latter portion of the penultimate paragraph of page 8 of the present memorandum, in which it is stated that the whole control of the chief of the local section of the General Staff by his own government must be accepted from the outset.
My hon. friend has also discussed the use of the Staff College at Camberley. This memorandum appears to contemplate the possibility of the Staff College at Camberley, which must for some years to come be the central school for the training of higher officers, becoming congested should a large number of officers from overseas be sent there, and the suggestion is made that there should be decentralization by the establishment of similar colleges in the overseas dominions. The Minister of Militia says:
In view of the improbability of any large increase of the Canadian Permanent Forces for some years to come, it is unlikely that the Dominion would for a considerable period, be able to spare more than four officers of that force at any one time for a Staff College training. If this be so, then it would not be worth while for the Dominion to establish a Staff College of its own, and it would be preferable, subject to War Office concurrence, to continue to send these officers to the Staff College, Camberley, following the existing arrangement.
My hon. friend does not read the part of the order in council *where we undertake to share in the expenditure.

Would my hon. friend tell me what particular page and clause (it is? My hon. friend knows the document thoroughly. At any rate I give my hon. friend credit for knowing that we could not make a subscription to the Camberley college without a vote of parliament.
I know that.

Well, my hon. friend has full opportunity of discussing it wdien that item of the Estimates is presented to parliament, he can then take the sense of the House upon it and if his opinions obtain and are those that animate the mass of the people the government would be defeated, the government would have to go out upon the question and my hon. friend Would come in.

My hon. friend, I admit, is perfectly right in the principle he lays down. What I questioned was the propriety of promising by order in council, without authority of parliament, to contribute to the support of the college at Camberley.
The order in council could not commit the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The order in council might commit the government, but could not commit the country. The people of the country and the members of parliament have an opportunity and must have an opportunity of turning the government out if they do not approve of their action.
No doubt about that.
And the opportunity must necessarily come before one single cent of Canadian money, could be spent on the college at Camberley, or any one of the objects outlined in this memorandum.
In other words, we would have to vote non-confidence in the government before that was set aside.
Would that be such a hard thing for the hon. gentleman?
It would.
It would be hard?
After the engagement taken by the order in council.
I think my hon. friend could bring himself up to that point without great difficulty.
I am better than my hon. friend thinks.

I know that he and some hon. gentlemen ride up to the fence with great courage and vim, spurring their horses with great activity, but when they get to the fence they sometimes funk it, and I am inclined to think that if he did not himself funk the fence a great many men around him would funk it and would not be prepared to say that Canada should not spend anything in regard to this plan of contribution to the college for the general staff.
My hon. friend I think is unfair. What I argued was that the plan was an important one with details and we should have been consulted before the government accepted it.

I cannot agree to my hon. friend's doctrine, but that was not really the question at issue between my hon. friend and the Prime Minister ; the question at issue was that the hon. gentleman had laid before the people of Quebec especially in many recent speeches a statement that the Prime Minister had created a misconception in the minds of the people and that he had suppressed facts which the people ought to have known. I have proved conclusively by the dates I have given that that accusation falls absolutely to the ground. I am not very surprised at the hon. gentleman's action in this regard. I do not accuse him of deliberate misrepresentation of the Prime Minister, I rather accuse him of not having known the facts which to-day he does know.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) said that he was subject to dreams, and I am not at all sure that some of his'statements to-night are not made of the stuff that dreams are made of.. The hon. gentleman talked a good deal about the unfair accusations made against him and others in connection with the Drummond-Arthabaska election, and while I do not know much about the statements made by gentlemen on one side or tin other in that campaign, I do know that if the statement made a while ago by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) about the Prime Minister is a fair specimen of the representations made to the people of Drummond-Arthabaska I do not wonder that the electors were deceived and led astray. I know my French Canadian citizens very well; I know their history. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) said they were not fickle, and they are not. They are loyal, patriotic citizens of this country and of this empire. They are a people who oyer and over again have shown themselves inaccessible to prejudiced appeals to their passions, when they have understood the situation and the real truth of the matter. I believe that in the Drummond-Arthabaska election the electors who voted non-confidence in this government on account of its naval

policy did not understand that naval policy and that they voted under a misconception in consequence of statements made to them with regard to that policy which were utterly devoid of truth. I was surprised, I was astonished beyond measure at the remark which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) made in regard to the history of the Prime Minister, and especially in connection with the campaign of 1896. The hon. gentleman exclaimed: How did Laurier arrive in power on that occasion?
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

' Hear, hear/ say hon. gentlemen opposite, but most of them who say * hear, hear ' are so young in political life that they probably do not know much about the matter. However, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) cannot plead ignorance, for it was in that campaign that he took his first plunge into political warfare and was first elected to this House. And on what platform was he elected? He was elected on the platform of the then Tory leaders; that Laurier had betrayed the people of the province of Quebec in connection with the Manitoba school question. Does he not remember very well the prophesies and the hopes and the anticipations that he and his fellow-Conservatives from Sir Charles Tupper down, had in regard to that election of 1896. It was common report throughout Canada that the Tory party was going to sweep Laurier out of existence in the province of Quebec, and why? Because they said he had betrayed his fellow-citizens of the province and had supported an improper school system in Manitoba. We have heard hon. gentlemen opposite charge that the Prime Minister has changed his course, and that he has spoken in one place differently from what he has spoken in another, but the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier knows full well that before the elections of 1896 the Prime Minister went down to his own constituents in the city of Quebec-leader that he was, great leader that he was, great statesman that he was-and in the city of Quebec he told his people that he would leave the school question in Manitoba to be dealt with by the people of Manitoba, because it was a provincial matter, and that he would not support the Remedial Bill to coerce Manitoba, which had been introduced by Sir Charles Tupper 'in the House of Commons. The right hon. gentleman took his political life in his hands and he said to his people: You must do what is right for the whole people of Canada, and he appealed to the French Canadian electors of the province of Quebec on the ground of right and justice, and they responded to that appeal on the 20th of June, 1896. And, Sir, the hopes of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier and his friends were disappointed, and instead of their getting a large majority in the province of Quebec to save them from defeat, Sir Wilfrid Laurier so demonstrated to his fellow-citizens of that province their duty to the country, in opposition to the fanatical appeals that -were made to them, that the French Canadian people, in opposition to their natural instincts and inclinations to vote in favour of their co-religionists, gave to the Liberal party a splendid majority, which contributed largely to put the right hon. gentleman in power. The hon. member (Mr. Monk) talks about the Prime Minister saying one thing in one place and another thing in another place.
Hear, hear.

' Hear, hear,' say those gentlemen opposite, but they do not know much about the history of the Prime Minister. Surely these gentlemen from the province of Ontario ought to remember another incident in the Life of the right hon. the leader of this government. They will call to memory the equal rights agitation in the province of Ontario, when the people -of Quebec were attacked, when they were accused of subservience to the church, when they were accused of selling to the church the rights of the people of Canada. I can remember, when the present Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Mr. Laurier, -went from here to the city of Toronto, right into the heart of that equal rights agitation, right into the centre of those who were arousing prejudices against the people of Quebec and against the Catholics of the Dominion, and he stood face to face with them there and the audience, which was hostile in the beginning, was so convinced by his eloquence and his arguments and his cogent reasoning, that before the meeting closed he held them in the hollow of his hand and every word he uttered was cheered to the echo as never before.
Was that the time when, quoting from Shakespeare, he told a Toronto audience that no Italian priest should tithe or toll in this fair Dominion, and when he told them in Quebec the exact reverse?
He never told them that.
Certainly he did.

I tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) that I heard the right hon. gentleman speak at both places and he uttered exactly the same sentiments at both. And his grand record, and the position which he occupies not only in Canada, but in the empire to-day is because the right hon. gentleman is equal and fair and just to everybody, no matter to what race they may belong. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) spoke about what he called ' our ' party, and I looked at the hon. gentleman

when he used that expression. I would be rather disposed to ask him what he means by 'our party.' Immediately afterwards he spoke about the Tory party and about the leader of the opposition, and one would suppose that by ' our party ' he meant the Conservative party.
If I used that word, I referred to those who made the campaign in favour of autonomy last summer in the province of Quebec.

Then my hon. friend means himself, those who sit with him here, and his allies of the Nationalist party. He uses the plural, our party, not mine; therefore there must be two parts to the party, and if one part is composed of those who sit with him and work with him in this House, I can only suppose that when the hon. gentleman alludes to ' our party,' he means the combination of the French Tories of Quebec with the Nationalists of Quebec. Only a little while ago the hon. leader of the opposition told us very distinctly that he and those for whom he spoke had no alliance with the Nationalists. He evidently did not speak for my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, and he ought rather to have said, 'I and some of those on this side^ of the House have no alliance with the Nationalist party.'
_ I think the people understand the position better than my hon. friend.
Possibly, but at the same time when my hon. friend talks to the people all over the country, I think he will find it very hard to make them understand his position.
No danger of that.
There is no danger of his talking all over the country.
There is more than you think.

I think my hon. friend will be very apt to come to the ground be-between two stools, on the one hand, the Conservative party, and on the other hand the Nationalist party; and when, as I believe will be the case in the near future, the Nationalist party of to-day follows the other parties which have risen and flitted across the horizon for a short time in the province of Quebec and then disappeared, my hon. friend will lose his allies of the Nationalist party and will not be able to take up again with his allies of the Tory party. However, my hon. friend has chosen his part. He or his ally Mrl Bourassa has had a temporary triumph. I thought it was a little significant, however, that when the other day my hon.. friend from Jacques Cartier and my hon.'

friend from L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) introduced Mr. Gilbert, the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska, into this House, he received rather a cool welcome. My hon. friend from Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel) smiles. He was down in Drummond and Arthabaska. My hon. friend from Champlain (Mr. Blondin), I think was there also. They helped to elect the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska; but when he was introduced to the House, even these ardent friends had not the courage or the good fellowship to give him a welcome. In the many years of experience that I have had in this House I have never before seen a member introduced without one signal of sympathy or of welcome.
I am surprised at my hon. friend, with his mighty mind, descending to these details.	'

My hon. friend went there first, and I am following him. Of all these representatives of the people of Canada, I can fairly say, not of their opinion of the personality of the hon. member, but of their opinion of the programme and platform on which he was elected, that there was none so poor to do him honour.
Now, I want to say a word or two in regard to some things in the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). That hon. gentleman said that he stood by his resolution of 1909 and by' every word of the speech which he made on that resolution. I am very glad that he does. I wish he would show it a little more by his actions rather than by his words, because I want to say, in compliment to the hon. member, that there were some things in that speech that I agreed with most thoroughly, and there was a line of argument in it with regard to the advantage of a Canadian navy manned by Canadians and belonging to the people of Canada, which had not been more eloquently or more beautifully expressed by anybody. Since then the hon. member for North Toronto has changed his mind; but I want to read one or two sentences of what he then said, and they are a most eloquent and beautiful expression of the action of the present Liberal government and of what the people of Canada have been doing since that time. I first take, on page 3495 of ' Hansard,' what he said about the objections to a fixed money contribution :
It bears the aspect of hiring somebody else
to do what we ourselves ought to do	
After ten or twelve, or twenty, or thirty years, you will have paid out an immense amount of money. You will have been protected in the meantime; but in Canada itself there will be no roots struck, there will be no residue left, there will be no preparation of the

soil, or beginning of the growth of the product of defence. Yet some time or other, no one can doubt that with resources and with a population constantly increasing, we must and will have in this country a naval force of our own for our coast and home defence.
The interest that we take in a contribution spent by another is not the interest that I desire for Canada. I want to see something graf-ed on the soil of Canada's nationhood, which takes root and grows and develops until it incites the spirit of defence in this country, leads to a participation in the defence, leads to that quick interest in it, its glories, its duties and its accomplished work, which is after all the one great thing that compensates a people for great expenditures either on land or on sea in the way of defence and of the maintenance of the rights of the country.
That is very good-excellent, eloquent, splendid sentences. He said further:
We must have beginnings; these must at first be small; hut some time, or other, as I have said, our country will have its naval force for the defence of this country if for nothing else. The point with me is as to whether it is not the greater wisdom to sow the seed at once and cultivate its growth, as best we may, in our circumstances and with our resources, until at last we arrive at that stage of expansion which we have reached in other great lines of our country's progress. You will notice that while 1 have tried to discuss the pros and cons in connection with this method, while I have stated reasons in favour of and others against it, my own mind tends rather towards the employment of another form than that of an out and out money contribution.
I agree emphatically with all those words. That has been exactly the action of the government. The government believes all these things. Consequently, it is making one of these small beginnings, and it is going on to greater things as we become able to organize and manage this force. My hon. friend, however, sneers at the efforts of the government. My hon. friend may not himself 'have used the words tin-pot navy, but at all events he has taken comfort out of the use of them by other people. I do not think my hon. friend will say to-day that either the ' Niobe ' or the ' Rainbow ' is a tin-pot vessel. If he does think so he thinks that Great Britain, which sold us these vessels, handed us a gold brick. I can hardly believe that he really holds that opinion. We bought those vessels exactly in pursuance of the policy and course the hon. gentleman himself laid down, but he has since changed his views and taken another course. Now he says that these are tin-pot vessels and that we have been deceived by the English lords of the admiralty. How, then, can the hon. gentleman, if he really holds that view, justify liis policy of sending a contribution of twenty or twenty-five million dollars Canadian money to the mother land to be controlled and expended by
these men, who, he says, have so flagrantly taken us in. The hon. gentleman expressed great disdain of the ' Rainbow,' and he asked if we would rather have the ' Rainbow ' than the British fleet to protect our shores in British Columbia should war break out on the Pacific. Well, we would have just the same protection of the British fleet, if such a war should break out, as if we had not the ' Rainbow.' We would have just the same protection as if we had sent money to Great Britain to pay for a Dreadnought. Even if we had sent money to the British admiralty to build a Dreadnought, does the hon. gentleman say that it would'be stationed on the Pacific coast? He knows perfectly well that the only reason for the sending of money to pay for a Dreadnought was the German scare, and that the intention was not to station her on the Pacific to strengthen the British fleet in the North Sea against aggression by that country. But let me tell my hon. friend that within a year or so when we have two or three Bristols on the Pacific coast we shall have vessels superior to any vessels in the Pacific ocean, with the exception of some of the finest Japanese ships. We shall not then have reason to fear any attack. In that very ' speech to which I have referred the hon. gentleman urged that it would be advisable for us to have some protection on our coasts in case of an attack by some cruiser should a war break out. Well, when we have, as we propose to have, on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts a couple of Bristols, we can rest assured lhat any stray cruiser, I care not from what navy, will be rendered a good account of by our Canadian navy.
The hon. gentleman said that we ought to read the resolution passed in 1909 from its genesis. What was its genesis? I will do him the compliment of saying that it was his own resolution, which he moved, and which was to this effect:-
That in the opinion of this House, in view of her great and varied resources, of her geographical position and national environments, and of that spirit of self help and self respect which alone befits a strong and growing people, Canada should no longer delay in assuming her proper share of the responsibility and financial burden incident to the suitable protection of her exposed coast line and great seaports.
When the hon. gentleman moved that resolution he certainly did not contemplate Canada taking any part in helping the empire except by protecting her own coasts. He did not then contemplate anything like a contribution to the imperial navy. That was brought in as an afterthought, and if we are to take this resolution in its final form, from the genesis in the brains of hon. gentlemen opposite, there was nothing imperial in its character, but it was simply for the protection of Canada and Canada alone.

My hon. friend seemed to imply that the final resolution was not to be lived up to, but I have pointed out that we have lived up to the picture which he drew and in which we all concurred and which was embodied in the final resolution. In that final resolution there is the possibility of an emergency, and the hon. gentleman dwelt strongly upon that, though not quite so strongly as did his leader. He asked what were we doing to meet an emergency, how could we help the mother land? But suppose we were to contribute money to build a Dreadnought, you cannot build a vessel of that kind in a day. It would take considerable time to build it. But, he said, the Canadian navy could be stronger than it is and help the empire as well. Well, it would take just the same time to build a Dreadnought for Canada as for the imperial navy. It would take just the same time to develop those ships and have them manned by Canadians. They would have to be manned by British sailors and officered by British officers whether the money was contributed direct to the British navy or expended on a Canadian navy. The conditions are exactly the same and the emergency would be met in exactly the same way.
My hon. friend is a past master in the art of word painting. There is a modern school of painting which reminds me of the hon! gentleman's policy. In his word pictures the technique is magnificent, the strokes are firm and bold, he does not hesitate to lay the colours on most daringly, and mixes them up frequently with violent and extraordinary contrasts. He reminds me of that modern school of painters known as the impressionist school. That is a school which lays down the principle that the artist must transfer to the canvas, not nature as she is, but as the artist thinks she is. The artist must put on canvas what his inner consciousness reveals to him regardless of actual appearances and facts. Accuracy, truth to nature and to fact, are foreign to this school. And my hon. friend, in his glorious word painting-which is very attractive and sounds remarkably well -reminds me very much of that school of artists and painters. He draws beautiful pictures. He works on them with the greatest diligence. They are very elaborate, very painstaking-long drawn out sometimes-but when it comes to the question of whether a picture is true to nature or not, or onlV true to the vivid imagination of the one who draws it, I venture to say that my hon. friend is following the teaching of the impressionist school of painting.
I will look it up.

The hon. gentleman may not know much about the impressionist school, but he is a past master in their art and emulates in his own way the great-Mr. FIStlER.
est members of the school. But the hon. gentleman has fallen away from what he started out with in dealing with this question of our naval service. He has changed very much, but in one thing he will never change, and that is in his determination to vote for whatever his leader may put before the House.
A question on the order paper to that effect will be answered in due time.

' In due time ' he says. ' Due time ' if he knows anything, is now. If he does not know what he should know as Minister of Railways that is all right, I am quite willing to accept his ignorance. I want an answer to this question, because it is only a prelude to other questions that I want to ask him. If this is a government work, I want to ask tlie minister why is this bridge being built on the Canadian Northern railway right-of-way?
For the simple reason that it is not.

Now I have the minister's answer : ' For the simple reason that it is not.' I want to tell the minister that while he was there, and should know, and does know, he is not" answering that question according to the facts of the case. It is built absolutely on the Canadian Northern railway right-of-way, on plans approved by himself and by the



Railway Commissioners. He can't denyi it, let him deny it if he can.
The minister's statement has to he accepted.
My statement is absolutely correct.
Withdraw.

I will withdraw nothing.
Some ihon. MEMBERS. Let him go on.

I appreciate your kindness very much. We all heard of the minister's trip up to the Pas Mission, when he went up there and had a little pow-wow with the Indians and the settlers, and where he dug out the first sod, was it- or was it the first nail he drove in this bridge? I want to tell the minister that the people up in that country are most anxious for the Hudson Bay railroad, the people of the whole Northwest are more than anxious for it. But they want it built by the people and controlled by the people. They don't want it handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, or the Canadian Northern railway or the Canadian Pacific railway. They want a road over which the people will have some control of the rates. If the Minister of Railways does not do what the people up there want, I can tell him that" if it was a sod that he dug, it is the first sod of the grave of the Liberal party in that country ; and if was a nail that he drove, it was the first nail in his own coffin.
What a sad case.

I referred to the fact that this bridge at the Pas is being built on the Canadian Northern railway right-of-way, according to plans that the minister has in his office. I now say that the bridge is being built in a straight line from the end of the rails on the Canadian Northern railway from the Hudson Bay Junction up to the Pas. But that line was built practically with the peoples' money, 90 miles from Hudson Bay Junction up to the Pas Mission. That 90 miles was guaranteed by the Saskatchewan government to the extent of $13,000 per mile, it was built through muskeg and swamp and rocks and dwarf timber, most of the way through a country that is practically worthless. This government also subsidized it to the extent of 20 square miles per mile, a little over a million acres, given by the people of Canada to build a line up there. The line is not ballasted, only one train or so a week runs over it, it is absplutely worthless to the people cxf Canada to-day. The only possibility of making use of that line is to utilize that bridge which is being -built by the people of this country and build a Mr. CAMPBELL.
line further on, and the minister says that is not the intention.
I did not say anything of the kind.

The Minister disclaims having said anything of the kind. I made the statement that it was built on the Canadian Northern Railway right of way. He disclaimed that, but it is built there. Absolutely the logical conclusion is that the bridge will be utilized for the purposes of that railway. The people have given over 1,000,000 acres of land for its building and the Saskatchewan government have given a guarantee of $13,000 per mile. If, under the most progressive government which we have in Manitoba, the boundary of our province had been extended at the time we asked for their extension, we would have had the road built to Hudson bay now and in operation. And I wish further to point out that the Conservatives have always been fighting for that road to Hudson bay. The Norquay government of Manitoba in 1888 gave a guarantee of bonds to build the road. They were defeated at the polls in that year and the Greenway government came into power. The Greenway government, a Liberal government, repudiated those bonds. I shall quote from the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' of that year a despatch from Ottawa, dated December 24, bearing out this statement. That despatch reads:
I learn from the Dominion government that the coolness of the Manitoba government regarding the construction of the Hudson Bay road will not warrant them to give a Dominion guarantee of the company's railway bonds. This is no doubt an excuse on their part, but as one minister said it is well taken. ' If.' said he, ' the local government of Manitoba have no confidence in the railway, and from their actions seemingly they have not, how could we pretend to know more than they concerning the matter. The road will now have to wait until local traffic develops to such an extent as to demand its construction.' I may say the government here are delighted over the action of the Green way government in refusing the guarantee of the road made by the Norquay government, and are quietly making considerable political capital from the course pursued. Hitherto Sir John Macdonald and his colleagues professed to be staunch supporters of the Hudson Bay railway scheme, but now see no good in aiding the enterprise in which the local administration have no confidence.
Another despatch in the same paper, the ' Free Press,' says:-
An offer from James Ross, of Montreal, and Mr. Onderdonk, of New York, to complete the Hudson Bay railway in two years, for a guarantee of $4,500,000. This was refused by the Greenway government, who manifested great hostility to the project. If it had not been for this opposition the road would have been built and in operation years ago.

I cite this to show that if there is fault it does not lie with the Conservative party. They have been anxious and at all times willing to do everything in their power to further the building of that road at the request of the people.
I wish to speak on many other things to-night, for probably two hours, but it is late, and I have compassion on you, Mr. Speaker, as sometimes you do not have on me. I must, however, refer to the recent election in Drummond and Arthabaska. I am sure you are tired of listening hour after hour
Sure.

An hon. gentleman said ' sure.' Is" it the Minister of Marine and Fisheries? I am glad that he confesses that he wasted hour after hour discussing a matter that is dead and past. He shows that he is sore, that the result of the election hurt his feelings, that he felt he had to make excuses for himself. The first time I spoke I reminded him of the old adage: ' qui s'excuse s'aoeuse.' When a man makes an excuse for himself you may be certain he has something to be ashamed of. The world of Shakespeare, The lady doth protest too much methinks,' are true in regard to that minister. I was surprised to see him for nearly an hour absolutely defame the people of his own province, his compatriots. He told the House that they were led astray, that they were fanatical, and anti-British in that if what he said about the Nationalists was true, then the people who voted for the Nationalists are as anti-British and fanatical as he claimed the Nationalists were. It was a surprise to me to hear it and I really do not believe it, because I have a great knowledge of these people. I will tell him why they voted against him. I believe the French Canadians are as intelligent and as loyal as any other of our people, that they have just as much reasoning power as any other people, and that they are like the rest of Canadians as would be shown if we had an election in any other province, they are just as wise to the fact that this government is being run by men who forget that they are not dictators, who use the people's money improperly, who refuse investigations when they are demanded and are absolutely unworthy of the confidence of the people of this country. That is the reason why the people of Drummond and Arthabaska voted against the Laurier candidate.
We hear from that side of the House all kinds of things about members on this side who took part with the Nationalists in that campaign; they have called them absolutely disloyal, they have read speeches out of Grit papers and claimed that our friends were disloyal. I throw it back to the Minister of Marine and his friends that the 21J	.
members on this side of the House were just as loyal as they can be on that side. Take Monsieur Bourassa, take his paper, Le Devoir,' what is it? It is his organ among whom? Among the English speaking people, not among the French. This is the organ that he uses to educate the the people of Quebec up to his ideas of Canadian politics. I will read what Mr. Bourassa says in ' Le Devoir ' which is circulated amongst French Canadians, and the same sentiments appeared in that newspaper before the election and during the election and after the election.
Read it in French.
I will read it in French or in Cree or in English or in any language you like. I quote from ' Le Devoir ' of October 22.
What year.

This year. Is that my old friend the Minister of Mines who woke up sufficiently to ask a question? This article says:-
J'irai plus loin-on accuse de faire appel aux sentiments de ma race-j'irai plus loin- si par inu] hon r la France venait attaquer nos rives, je serais le premier a dire: Canadiens-franpais, armez-vous et defendez le drapeau britannique, meme contre la France.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will translate that for you.
Hear, hear.

I want every man in this House to understand that this is the kind of sentiments that Mr. Bourassa, the leader of the Nationalist party in Canada places before his French Canadian citizens. I translate as follows from 'Le Devoir' :-
I would go further; I am accused of making an appeal to the sentiments of my race. If by chance France would attack our shores I would be the first to say, French Canadians arm yourselves and defend the British flag even against France.
Oh.
Some one over there said 'oh.' I have no doubt that language makes you sick because it shows you that Bourassa is a loyal subject of the British Empire.
He says: Arm yourselves and I will stay at home.
That's where you ought to stay. Then Mr. Bourassa goes on to say.
What is that?

I am speaking of Mr. Bourassa. My hon. friend does not seem to have any common sense, and I would be pleased to put some into him if I had the opportunity. Mr. Bourassa goes on to say,

that if his own children were big enough he would be willing to sacrifice them on the altar of the British Empire, and yet some hon. gentlemen opposite say that Bourassa is disloyal. Well, that is the kind of loyalty that appeals to me, and I am not afraid to acknowledge it. I don't approve of Mr. Bourassa's policy with regard to the navy and I never did. I am a Conservative of a sort of independent type, first, last and all the time. I am something more than that for I believe absolutely in imperial federation. And, Sir, if you will eliminate the Conservative party and its naval policy altogether, forget the Conservative party, forget that they have a policy of that kind, and then take the Liberal policy and the Nationalist policy, and I will vote every time to go to the people and ask them for their mandate before I would build a tin-pot navy that would never be any use. What use is it? In time of peace we don't need it and in time of war it's no good. Just imagine a navy with the Minister of Marine at the head of it. Why, he cannot run the buoys that he has floating ar.ound to mark dangerous shoals. He asks us to entrust him with the running of the navy, but was not the 'Arctic' and the 'Montcalm' and the 'Minnie M.' enough for him? If he runs this navy at the same rate of expenditure as he ran these three old boats it will ruin the people of Canada, and the sooner the navy is blown up the better. Well, I heard stories about the Drummond-Arthabaska election, as well as those we heard from the other side of the House. I heard about the speech of the First Minister at that packed convention in Montreal, that subsidized convention where those who attended were paid four dollars apiece. Speaking in his flowery language to that assembled mob of paid supporters the Prime Minister said: I will accept the decision of Drummond-Arthabaska as the decision of Quebec as to whether they want me or not. Well, he has got his answer and just as sure as he said it, that verdict has gone into the hearts of the people of Canada and he is on the toboggan slide, and we will keep him there. Our friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) reprimanded everybody who was against him but he did not point to his own little shortcomings. In one speech at Victoriaviile he told the people: If you vote for Laurier you are voting for a Canadian navy and if you vote for Borden you are voting for an imperial navy and just as sure as Borden is elected conscription will come. He was the first man of the whole campaign that said anything of that kind and if he is here let him deny it if he can.
He made no such statement.
Do you know anything about it? '
Certainly, I know everything about it.

I told you the substance of what he said, and as most of the papers down there are Grit papers you can't believe them. Our friend the Solicitor General was in that election, and if the gentleman sitting beside him would wake him up I would like to direct some attention to him. The hon. gentleman sat in an office or a room down in Victoriaviile for several days during that campaign, if I am rightly informed. What was he doing, Sir? He was there with the avowed purpose of settling claims. What were the claims? Claims for an old horse of a Liberal supporter which was hired in the general election and got wounded or died-$400 for that; some hay claims, I guess, to feed the dead horse; little settlements for rigs hired to go here and there. The Solicitor General is in his place, and, if my information is correct he might lay on the table a statement of the exact claims he did settle, the amounts of them, and what amounts are still outstanding.
Mr. Speaker, if I cannot lay it on the table, I can give it the flattest denial possible.
I did not quite catch what the hon. gentleman said.
My hon. friend is misinformed. The statement is absolutely untrue.	.	.
Then, the hon. gentleman was not there settling claims-am I to understand that?
I was not there settling claims.

Mr. Speaker, what was he there for-to beat poor Perrault?-because that was the result. I would like to pay a little tribute to the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) in passing. He told the House that he was the first man on the ground when that election came on, and the last to leave-and he takes credit to himself-for what? A majority of 1,200 for the gentleman who last represented Drummond and Arthabaska in this House, and 270 now on the other side, a change of nearly 1,500, and he said that if he had been there ten days longer he thought he could have won out. Anybody who knows anything about arithmetic knows that if he had stayed ten days longer, Mr. Perrault would have lost his deposit. I heard a story about my friend from Hochelaga (Mr. Rivet) on the eve of the election, which I think would be interesting for you, Mr. Speaker, to hear. Our friend received a hurry-up call. A meeting was to be held at a certain house, and the hon. member went to attend the

meeting. It was more or less successful for both sides. There were ladies present, and after the meeting the ladies were treated by our friend from Hoehelaga to wine and peanuts-peanuts, Mr. Speaker. What lady would be tempted by a bribe of that kind? Our friend the First Minister was out in British Columbia last summer. He was well received there. He was received by the whole Conservative party of the province. I may say that British Columbia, with almost no exception, is Conservative. We have one of the exceptions here, or two of them, and when I point out to the members these exceptions, they can easily realize that the exception proves the rule. The First Minister was treated in the proper manner by the Conservatives, and in moving up the aisle to the dais that was built for him in the big reception hall, he was heard to say, looking around:	'This is paradise.' I am
sure that when he thinks of the Drummond and Arthabaska election he must say right down in his heart: ' This is purgatbry.' It is my earnest wish that he may long remain there-I only speak politically, because I was taught some scripture, and I realize that at the eleventh hour the greatest sinner may return. There were many other things, Sir, I wanted to bring to your attention, but I have some compassion on you; and, if permitted, I will close with a quotation which I think is most apt. I read ' it on Sunday when I was in my room looking over the good book. You will find it in Matthew, the 15th chapter, and the 7th verse. I think it applies to the Liberal party as constituted to-day, with their professions of loyalty, better than anything else:
Ye hyprocrites well did Isias prophecy of you saying, this people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth and honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

G.	T. R. TRAINMEN'S STRIKE.

Did the government make an arrangement with the Grand Trunk railway and its trainmen and conductors that all would be reinstated within a period of ninety days, as a basis of settlement of recent strike? If so, why has that agreement not been carried out?

The agreement which was the basis of settlement of the recent strike was made between the parties to the dispute and not between the government and the parties. Section 1 of that agreement provided that:-
* 1. The company will put back as soon as possible the men other than those who have been or may be found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct, the understanding being that there is to be no coercion or intimidation used towards the ' new men.'

An assurance was given by the company that by the words, 'as soon as possible' in this section was meant a period not exceeding three months from the date of the settlement. In a communication dated November 10, Mr. Hays, president of the company, says:-
' In the opinion of the officers of this company our undertaking to re-employ all who were not found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct has been complied with.'
-The government has been informed by the representatives of the men that they take the position that the officers of the company have not carried out that part of the agreement; the government has so informed Mr. Hays and has strongly urged a re-consideration of the cases of all men involved in the recent strike who have not as yet been restored to the company's service.

1.	The schedules for the census of 1911 consist of thirteen regular schedules for use in all organized provinces of the Dominion, and three special schedules for use in the Northwest Territories, and were published in the ' Canada Gazette ' of July 9, 1910.
The thirteen regular schedules relate to the subjects of:-
1.	Population by name, personal description. etc.
2.	Mortality, disability and compensation.

3.	Heads of families, post office addresses, houses and buildings, occupied land, fruit trees and their products.
4.	Grain and other field crops for the harvest year 1910.
5.	Hoed crops, tobacco, hops and grass seeds in 1910, and field crop areas in 1911.
6.	Animals and animal products.
7.	Farm and urban values.
8.	Forest products in 1910.
9.	Manufactures.
10.	Churches, schools, colleges and other institutions.
11.	Fisheries.
12.	Butter and cheese factories.
13.	Mining and mineral products.
The three special schedules relate to population and mortality and the production of furs and skins, and of fish, whales and seals in the Northwest Territories.
2.	The subjects of inquiry are practically the same for the census years 1910 and 1911; but for the latter year there are questions relating to life and accident insurance, and to accidents and disability and compensation in cases of accidents during the census year.
3.	There are no essential changes in the schedule of manufactures, but in the proceedings of enumeration it is proposed to have the census of 1911 taken by the regular enumerators instead of by special agents as in 1901.
4.	Except as specially provided in the instructions, the census of industries will be limited to establishments employing not less than five persons at any period of the census year. Industries such as saw mills, flour mills, dairy factories, brick and tile works, fish curing plants, etc., specified in the instructions, will be taken whether the number of persons employed is less or more than five.
